edits.quote: Shape Detectives!
edits.fix: Delete the second page title; the running header is enough.

edits.quote: Today you’ll become a shape detective and discover how pieces fit together!
edits.fix: Delete. If shared rules are wanted, put one unnumbered line at the top: 'Fill each shape with pattern blocks. Turn pieces to fit. No gaps, no overlaps, nothing sticking out.'

edits.quote: Fill the sailboat and the cat. Use any small pieces.
edits.fix: Give the problem a goal so it isn't done in a minute (the sailboat is 11 triangle spaces, the cat 7): 'Fill the sailboat and the cat with as few pieces as you can.' The sailboat takes 4 pieces at best (a hexagon across the sail and hull, 2 blues, 1 green).

edits.quote: Great job! You’re a tiling superstar!
edits.fix: Delete.

edits.quote: Ask an adult to trace your pieces before you lift them to use again.
edits.fix: Delete it from the student page. Each shape is printed twice and there are plenty of blocks, so nothing has to be lifted. If tracing is wanted as a record, put it in the adult notes.

edits.quote: Fill each shape two different ways. (Hexagon outline is exactly one yellow hexagon; Diamond is a 2-by-2 rhombus.)
edits.fix: Placing one yellow block 'fills' the hexagon, and a second way takes seconds. Rewrite as the classic K–1 counting problem: 'How many different ways can you fill the hexagon?' (8 different mixes of pieces, from 1 yellow to 6 greens). Print 8 hexagon outlines at actual size in the empty lower part of the page, and drop the second diamond.

edits.quote: Hexagon / Diamond (subheadings above the board pairs)
edits.fix: Delete the subheadings. The outlines identify themselves; keep at most one small label under each board.

edits.quote: Turn the pieces as needed. Use them again for the next shape.
edits.fix: Delete. Turning was already allowed in P1, and reusing pieces needs no instruction.

edits.quote: Hint: Start at the pointy tip of the arrow and work your way in.
edits.fix: Delete. The arrow is just two chevrons side by side, so the hint gives away the only step and adds nothing.

edits.quote: Fill the arrow and the star using only small purple chevrons.
edits.fix: The arrow has 1 solution with 2 pieces, so it is over almost at once. The star has exactly 2 chevron fillings. Ask 'Find two different ways to fill the star with chevrons' and print a second star, or add a third shape that chevrons cannot fill (for example the long hexagon from P4) and ask which shapes can be filled.

edits.quote: Bonus Challenge
edits.fix: Delete the label. P4 and P5 are easier than P3 and are not optional, so the label misleads as well.

edits.quote: Fill the long hexagon using only small blue rhombi. Then fill it again with any small pieces you like.
edits.fix: Make 'find all the ways' the task: 'Find every way to fill the long hexagon with blue rhombi.' There are exactly 3, so print 3 outlines at actual size. Delete the open-ended 'fill it again with any pieces you like', which has no goal or end point.

edits.quote: Fill the mountain using only small green triangles. Then fill it again with any small pieces you like.
edits.fix: Filling a side-3 triangle with 9 greens is busywork. Replace with 'Fill the mountain with as few pieces as you can' (the answer is 3 red trapezoids).

edits.quote: Packet ends after P5 (about 15 minutes of work for a quick K–1 child).
edits.fix: About 25 minutes are missing. Add a 'which can you fill?' problem with blue rhombi on 4–5 actual-size outlines, some fillable and some not (for example a side-2 triangle, the cat, a hexagon, and a 2-by-2 rhombus). This is an entry point to the 2–3 coloring idea.

edits.quote: Packet ends after P5 (second missing block).
edits.fix: Add a building problem that uses the upscale blocks: 'Build the big (2×) yellow hexagon out of small pieces. Use as few pieces as you can, then as many as you can,' or 'Which big (2×) block can you copy using only small blues?' Print outlines at actual size.

k-1.summary: The shapes are drawn correctly at actual size and every one can be filled, but the work is the watered-down kind the organizer has complained about: one yellow block fills P2's hexagon, P5 is nine greens, and a quick child is done in about 15 minutes. There is cutesy text throughout (title, intro, 'tiling superstar', 'Bonus Challenge', the arrow hint). Recasting the problems as 'how many ways' and 'fewest pieces' tasks and adding two substantial problems is over an hour of work.

edits.quote: The Great Board Mystery
edits.fix: Delete the second page title.

edits.quote: Remember: tiling isn’t just about filling space, it’s about seeing hidden patterns!
edits.fix: Delete. This is the 'not X, but Y' tic and does no work.

edits.quote: Boards A–D (A: side-3 triangle, 9 spaces; B: 2×3 parallelogram, 12; C: 11-space pentagon; D: long hexagon, 10)
edits.fix: The two boards that can't be filled (A and C) fail only because they have an odd number of spaces, so 'What is stopping you?' has the shallow answer 'odd count'. Replace C with an even-area board that has more up-triangles than down-triangles, so the real obstruction appears from the start. One example is the 1-over-3 trapezoid: 8 spaces, 5 up and 3 down, and blues leave 2 empty.

edits.quote: Which boards can you fill and which ones did you get stuck on? What is stopping you from completely filling some of the shapes?
edits.fix: 'Got stuck on' mixes up a failed attempt with impossibility. Ask: 'Which boards can’t be filled with blues? How do you know?'

edits.quote: Keep pieces inside the board without overlaps. / without overlaps or pieces outside / Keep pieces inside the triangle without overlaps. / Cover whole triangle spaces without overlaps or pieces outside.
edits.fix: The same rule is restated in every problem. State it once as an unnumbered shared rule at the top of page 1 and delete the repeats.

edits.quote: Hint: Color the triangles that point up and the triangles that point down, then count each kind.
edits.fix: Delete. It prints the central discovery of the activity, the coloring argument. Move it to the adult notes as a prompt for children who are stuck.

edits.quote: Record how many blues fit and how many triangle spaces stay empty.
edits.fix: Delete. The 'Blues: __ Empty spaces: __' blanks under each board already say this.

edits.quote: Use only small blue rhombi on these triangles and the triangle on the next page.
edits.fix: The problem is split across two pages with a cross-reference. Keep one statement ('Fit as many blue rhombi as you can on each triangle') and let the side-5 triangle continue on the next page under the same problem without restating it.

edits.quote: Problem 2: Fit as many small blue rhombi as you can in this triangle. Keep pieces inside the triangle without overlaps. Record your best packing.
edits.fix: Remove the duplicate 'Problem 2:' label and the restated instructions. Keep only the board, its blanks, and the closing question.

edits.quote: Record your best packing.
edits.fix: It is unclear whether this means drawing the rhombi on the grid or filling the blanks. Say 'Draw your best packing on the grid' or delete it.

edits.quote: Fewest empty triangle spaces: / Blues: ___ Purples: ___
edits.fix: There is one 'fewest empty' label with no blank, followed by two blanks that could mean piece counts or gap counts. Replace with two clear lines under each board: 'Blues only: empty spaces __' and 'Purples only: empty spaces __'. (Answers: A 0/0, B 0/4, C 0/0, D 0/2, E 1/1, F 2/4.)

edits.quote: Boards A and C (3-wide and 2-wide arrows)
edits.fix: These are the same example twice: blues and chevrons both fill each exactly. Replace C with a contrasting board, for example one where blues fill exactly and a chevron leaves 2 gaps for a different reason than B or D, or a larger board where the gap difference is bigger.

edits.quote: Can you cover one purple exactly with blues? How does this explain which pieces can leave fewer gaps?
edits.fix: The first question hands over the key step of the proof. Ask instead: 'Could purples ever leave fewer empty spaces than blues on some board? Explain.' Put the 'cover a purple with blues' prompt in the adult notes.

edits.quote: Closing question has no answer space; a grey Fun fact box fills the remaining space
edits.fix: Delete the box and add 3 ruled answer lines.

edits.quote: Fun fact: Mathematicians call this kind of argument a coloring proof!
edits.fix: Delete. It is also misplaced: the purple-versus-blue argument is a splitting argument, and the coloring argument belongs to P2.

edits.quote: Blank page 5 (no header, footer only)
edits.fix: Delete the empty trailing page.

edits.quote: Packet ends after P3 (a quick third grader runs out at about 30 minutes, roughly 10 short)
edits.fix: Add an invention problem on an actual-size triangle-grid sheet: 'Draw a board with an even number of spaces that blues cannot fill. Then draw one where blues must leave exactly 3 spaces empty.' Optionally add a prediction to P2: 'How many spaces would a triangle with 10 edges on each side leave empty?'

grades-2-3.summary: This is a real development of the coloring obstruction from the outline: impossible boards, fewest-gap packings of side-2 to side-5 triangles, and blues against chevrons. Every board is drawn correctly at actual size, and the answers check out (n gaps for side n; chevrons never beat blues). The edits: the printed hint and leading questions give the proofs away, P1's impossible boards are only odd-area, P3's recording blanks are ambiguous, there is AI slop (title, 'not X but Y', fun fact) and a blank last page, and a quick child is about 10 minutes short.

edits.quote: Welcome, tiling explorers! In this activity, you will discover the secret world of flips.
edits.fix: Delete.

edits.quote: Find as many different tilings as you can. ... How many different tilings did you find?
edits.fix: Make completeness the central question: 'Find all the tilings. How do you know there are no more?' (There are 6. Keep the 8 small boards so the count isn't given away.)

edits.quote: Make a map on these six cards. (Cards A–F print all six tilings directly after P1)
edits.fix: Anyone who turns the page sees P1's answer: exactly six tilings, all drawn. Print the six cards on a separate half-sheet handed out after P1, or have children cut out and letter their own P1 drawings as the map cards.

edits.quote: Can you get from every card to every other card by a sequence of flips? Explain your thinking.
edits.fix: Delete 'Explain your thinking.' Once the map is drawn, the answer can be read straight off it.

edits.quote: Find the shortest route from A to F. Write the cards you visit and count your flips. Explain your thinking.
edits.fix: With the map drawn, this takes about a minute (A-B-C-E-F or A-B-D-E-F, 4 flips) and is too slight to stand alone. Merge it into P4 as one routes problem and drop 'Explain your thinking.'

edits.quote: Part 2: Ribbons, the Secret Code
edits.fix: Delete the section heading.

edits.quote: At any step, is there a choice of which rhombus to cross next? Could one tiling have two different ribbons starting at the bold edge?
edits.fix: Filler follow-up whose answer is plainly 'no' from the definition. Move it to the adult prompts.

edits.quote: Problem 6: Draw the ribbon on each of these tilings. Write its code from bottom to top.
edits.fix: P5 (card B) and P6 (cards C–F) are one routine task, applying the same procedure five times, split into two numbered problems. Merge them into one problem: definition plus example on A, then B–F together. This also fills the empty lower half of page 3.

edits.quote: Follow these steps. (a) Count the L’s in each code. (b) Count the R’s in each code. (c) Add them up. (d) Look at how many edges the board has on its left and right sides, and use that to explain why.
edits.fix: Replace the steps with: 'What do all six codes have in common? Explain why every tiling’s code must be like that.' The steps print the discovery and its explanation, and 'explain why' never says what is to be explained.

edits.quote: Write every different order you can make with two L’s and two R’s. Match each order to a tiling card.
edits.fix: This is an unnumbered task inside P7, and the matching is a lookup because the codes were already written in P5–P6. Give it its own number and give it a purpose: 'List every order of two L’s and two R’s. Does each one come from exactly one tiling? What does that tell you about your answer to Problem 1?'

edits.quote: Rebuild the tiling from each ribbon. (Printed ribbons are RLLR and LLRR, i.e. cards D and F)
edits.fix: Both ribbons belong to cards D and F, which children just drew in P6, so the rebuild is a copy job and the question 'Can either ribbon give two different tilings?' is answered by looking at the cards. Give ribbons on a board they have not seen. One option is a hexagon with top 1 and slanted sides 3, where codes have three L’s and three R’s: rebuild from a code, then use codes to count all 20 tilings. This is the counting application from the outline.

edits.quote: Problem 10: Circle every neighboring RL or LR in your six codes. Can you make a flip at every circled pair? Are there any flips that do not come from one of these pairs?
edits.fix: P10 prints the rule that P9 ('What changes? Write three examples.') asks children to discover. Merge P9 and P10 into one open problem: 'How does one flip change a ribbon code? Find a rule that tells you, from the code alone, which flips are possible. Use it to explain your answer to Problem 4.' This also closes the parity loop from the outline, which the packet never connects.

grades-4-5.summary: This is the strongest band and it is mathematically correct throughout. The six cards are six distinct valid tilings of the 1-2-2 hexagon, the A↔B example is a real flip, and the printed ribbons and codes (A=RRLL, B=RLRL, C=LRRL, D=RLLR, E=LRLR, F=LLRR) all check, as do the shortest route (4 flips) and the even-return parity. The development of flips and ribbons follows the outline and gives a quick child 40+ minutes. It needs about 45 minutes of edits: the cards give away P1's count, P7 and P10 print the discoveries as steps, P8 rebuilds tilings already on the page, P3/P5/P6 are thin or split, and there is opening and section-heading slop.

overall.strongest: Grades 4–5: a correct, well-sequenced exploration of the 1-2-2 hexagon's six rhombus tilings, the flip map, shortest routes, parity, and ribbon codes, with accurate cards and enough work for a quick child.
overall.weakest: K–1: easy fill-the-outline tasks (one yellow block fills the 'hexagon', nine greens fill the 'mountain') wrapped in cutesy text; it runs out after about 15 minutes and needs two new substantial problems plus rewrites of P2, P4 and P5.
